lesson.menu_title: How Long Have You Been Doing That?
lesson.menu_desc: The house you are restoring and the things you tinker with -- present perfect continuous against present perfect simple
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 3 -- How Long Have You Been Doing That?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 3 -- How Long Have You Been Doing That?
lesson.grammar_point: present perfect continuous vs present perfect simple

listenings.text: People ask me how long I have been working on the house, and I always laugh, because the honest answer is nine years. Nine years for one house. When we bought it, the roof was worn out, the windows did not close, and there was carpet glued to a wooden floor that turned out to be beautiful underneath. I have finished the kitchen and both bedrooms. I have been working on the staircase since March and it is still not done. My husband says it is a labor of love, and he is right, although some weekends it feels like just labor. What I have learned is that you never restore a house. The house restores you. I am far more patient than I was nine years ago, and I have a knack for things I did not even know I could do.

My wife has been asking me the same question every Saturday for about three years. How long have you been out there? And the honest answer is usually four hours. I go into the garage to fix one thing and I come out at dinner time. I have always been into old radios. Not collecting them, mind you, repairing them. I have fixed maybe forty of them and I have given away almost all of them. People think it must be relaxing. It is not relaxing at all. It is painstaking, and half the parts do not exist anymore, so you salvage what you can. But when a radio that has been silent for sixty years starts playing, there is nothing like it. That is why I have never gotten around to selling any of them.
